messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: In women with Hashimoto's disease, depressive symptoms decreased with implementing dietary recommendations including consuming vitamin D-rich products.
Sentence: "Depression symptoms decreased with the implementation of some dietary recommendations, including the consumption of products rich in iodine, iron, zinc, selenium, vitamin D, vitamin A and polyunsaturated omega-3 fatty acids."
Measured as: depression symptoms (Beck Depression Scale)
Population: 219 women aged 20-50 with Hashimoto's disease
Intervention: Dietary behaviour of consuming vitamin D-rich products (self-reported, questionnaire)
Comparator: Less adherence to the dietary recommendation
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 219
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D status was not significantly associated with depressive symptoms in female nurses.
Sentence: "Vitamin D status was not significantly associated with EDS, anxiety symptoms, or depressive symptoms, whereas EDS was associated with both anxiety and depressive symptoms."
Measured as: depressive symptoms (HADS)
Population: Female nurses working at a university hospital, mean age 32.4 years
Intervention: Serum 25(OH)D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Higher vs lower vitamin D status
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

content.text: {"evaluation":"Study A's exposure is adherence to a multi-nutrient dietary pattern (vitamin D-rich foods among iodine, iron, zinc, selenium, omega-3 and others), not vitamin D itself, and the comparator is simply less adherence. That arguably makes the pair off_question, but the guide's list of off-question cases doesn't clearly cover a dietary pattern that names vitamin D, so a genuine verdict is defensible. All three responses chose genuine, so the ranking turns on reason and detail. Response C picks population (Hashimoto's vs nurses) as primary, which is a real difference but understates that the exposure is a food pattern versus measured serum level; it also says the results point 'opposite ways' and calls nurses 'healthy', neither of which the fields state. Responses A and B both choose intervention as primary, which better captures the exposure mismatch. Response B states the mismatch most cleanly (self-reported vitamin D-rich foods vs serum 25(OH)D) and keeps its detail accurate. Response A is similar but its detail runs two things together. Neither A nor B flags the possible off_question issue, so they are close, with B slightly better written. C ranks last for the weaker primary reason and the unsupported claims.","ranking":["B","A","C"]}
